scopedSubtopics.subtopic: Fossil Fuel Combustion and Energy-Related CO2 Emissions
scopedSubtopics.description: Burning of coal, oil, and natural gas for energy production, transportation, and heating. Represents approximately 75% of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and is the single largest driver of modern climate change.

scopedSubtopics.subtopic: Deforestation and Land Use Change Emissions
scopedSubtopics.description: Conversion of forests to agricultural land and urban areas eliminates carbon sinks and releases stored carbon. Tropical deforestation contributes 10-15% of global emissions while reducing CO2 absorption capacity.

scopedSubtopics.subtopic: Agricultural Methane and Nitrous Oxide Emissions
scopedSubtopics.description: Agriculture contributes 24% of global emissions through methane from livestock and rice cultivation, and nitrous oxide from fertilizers. Livestock alone accounts for 14.5% of global emissions.
Manufacturing of cement, steel, and chemicals involves chemical reactions that inherently release CO2 beyond energy-related emissions. Cement production alone accounts for 8% of global CO2 emissions.

scopedSubtopics.subtopic: Greenhouse Gas Properties and Radiative Forcing
scopedSubtopics.parentArea: Greenhouse Gas Properties and Radiative Forcing
scopedSubtopics.description: Different greenhouse gases have varying atmospheric lifetimes and warming potentials. Understanding radiative forcing quantifies each factor's contribution to warming and underpins climate models.

scopedSubtopics.subtopic: Climate Feedback Mechanisms and Tipping Points
scopedSubtopics.description: Self-reinforcing processes that amplify climate change including ice-albedo feedback, permafrost thaw releasing methane, and ocean CO2 release. These feedbacks can accelerate warming beyond initial forcing.

Transportation accounts for 16% of global emissions, with road vehicles contributing the majority. Aviation and shipping are particularly challenging to decarbonize due to energy density requirements.

Multiple lines of evidence including isotopic signatures, spatial patterns, and model attribution studies definitively establish that current warming is caused by human activities, not natural variability.

keyUncertainties.uncertainty: Precise quantification of feedback loop magnitudes and tipping point thresholds
keyUncertainties.impact: Determines whether climate change remains manageable or accelerates beyond human control, critical for setting emission reduction targets

keyUncertainties.uncertainty: Future natural carbon sink capacity under continued warming
keyUncertainties.impact: Affects how much additional CO2 can be absorbed by oceans and forests, influencing required emission reductions

keyUncertainties.uncertainty: Interaction effects between multiple climate drivers
keyUncertainties.impact: Non-linear interactions could amplify or dampen overall warming, affecting projection accuracy

keyUncertainties.uncertainty: Full accounting of supply chain and consumption-based emissions
keyUncertainties.impact: Current territorial accounting may misattribute emissions, affecting policy effectiveness and responsibility allocation
